strengths: Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over prior SOTA (80.2% vs 64.2% on AndroidWorld, 53.6% vs 41.2% on AndroidLab)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with proper ablation studies (Table 3c, Figure 3b) showing contribution of each component
Outperforms much larger proprietary models (72B parameters) with smaller open models (7B/9B)
Well-executed engineering contribution: distributed framework supporting 256+ parallel Android virtual devices
Thoughtful multi-stage design with reasoning SFT providing interpretable policy initialization
Good reproducibility: open-source release, detailed hyperparameters, extensive implementation details in appendices
Clear presentation with informative architecture diagrams and result visualizations
Evaluation across multiple benchmarks (AndroidWorld, AndroidLab, AndroidControl) and backbone models
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: ADAGRPO combines known techniques (experience replay, curriculum learning, reward shaping) without fundamental innovation
Reward model bias for AndroidLab: VLM-based reward model achieves only 86% accuracy; authors acknowledge bias from proprietary VLM majority voting
Best model (MOBILERL-9B) trained only on AndroidWorld while MOBILERL-7B trained on both, suggesting different configurations for different benchmarks
Narrow evaluation scope: Android-only, no evaluation on real public-use apps (acknowledged limitation), relatively small benchmarks (20 and 9 apps)
XML-based grounding is fundamental limitation: many popular apps lack sufficient accessibility information; eventually requires visual-only grounding (unaddressed)
Substantial resource requirements severely limit reproducibility: requires 4 CPU machines with 1TB memory, 256 parallel rollouts, 25+ hours for 100 training steps
Heavy dependence on SFT initialization: reasoning-free SFT alone provides +22.6% improvement, dominating RL gains of +15.2%
SPA shows smallest impact in ablations (+1.9% on AndroidWorld), with primary benefit in step efficiency rather than accuracy
Ad-hoc FCF design: threshold selection (2 consecutive failures, 3-epoch cooldown) lacks principled justification
Missing error analysis and limited discussion of which task types benefit from which components

strengths: Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over prior work (16% over UI-Tars-1.5 on AndroidWorld, 12.4% over UI-Genie-Agent on AndroidLab)
Practical distributed infrastructure contribution for large-scale Android device simulation with reproducibility
Comprehensive experimental details including extensive ablations by task complexity, step efficiency analysis, and detailed appendices with hyperparameters and data processing
Well-articulated problem motivation with three clear technical challenges: sparse signals, heavy-tailed task difficulty, and sampling bottlenecks
Promise to open-source the framework and commitment to reproducibility with detailed implementation details
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: SPA is straightforward length-based reward shaping without theoretical justification; AdaPR is standard experience replay (Mnih et al., 2015); FCF is authors' own 'simplified version of curriculum learning' with minimal innovation

Critical evaluation concerns preventing clear attribution of gains: (1) uses different base models (Qwen2.5-VL-7B, GLM-4.1V-9B) than baselines making isolation of algorithm contributions impossible, (2) AndroidLab relies on biased VLM-based reward model (acknowledged in Appendix E), (3) additional human annotation data and self-exploration provide unclear advantage, (4) inconsistent training setups (mixed training for Qwen, AndroidWorld-only for GLM)

Weak justification for design choices: Reasoning-Free SFT provides massive gains (+40% for GLM) with unexplained mechanism; SPA acknowledged to have 'smallest impact on overall accuracy'; hyperparameters (α=1.0, γ=1.0, κ=0.25) lack ablations; FCF threshold (2 consecutive failures) appears arbitrary

Narrow evaluation scope limited to Android emulators only (no real devices, public-use apps, or cross-platform evaluation); authors acknowledge inability to evaluate on out-of-domain apps due to 'lack of reproducible evaluation protocol'; fundamental limitation that apps with incomplete XML hierarchies (TikTok, etc.) cannot be handled

Incomplete and inconsistent ablations: reasoning-free SFT mechanism unexplained; no comparison with principled curriculum learning methods despite FCF being acknowledged as simplified version; image resolution switch (Table 6) creates confounds; SPA's benefits limited to step efficiency, not directly to success rate

Reproducibility challenges: extreme training time (100 steps = 25+ hours), dependence on proprietary VLMs for data annotation and reward models, privacy mechanisms may hinder code release, hyperparameter choices appear ad-hoc without systematic exploration

Presentation and clarity issues: Figure 2 cluttered and hard to parse; dense writing with many components introduced without sufficient intuition; related work on curriculum learning and reward shaping comes late and is superficial; overclaimed 'state-of-the-art' statements when gains partially attributable to better base models
Limited statistical rigor: main results lack clear statement of number of runs and confidence intervals; small test sets (116 tasks for AndroidWorld); no significance testing reported

strengths: Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over prior work (+16% on AndroidWorld to 80.2%, +12.4% on AndroidLab to 53.6%)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with well-designed ablations (Table 3c, Figure 3b) clearly showing contribution of each component
Practical engineering contribution: distributed framework supporting 256 concurrent Android devices addresses real scalability challenges
Thoughtful two-stage warm-up strategy with iterative reasoning refinement contributing 6-18% improvement
Thorough documentation and implementation details across main paper and extensive appendices supporting reproducibility
Solid experimental design including case studies, multi-benchmark evaluation, and complexity-based analysis (Figure 4)
Open-source framework release valuable for practitioners in mobile GUI agent development
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: SPA is straightforward reward scaling, AdaPR applies standard experience replay, FCF implements basic curriculum learning - contributions are primarily in combination rather than novel methods

Unclear attribution of improvements: Table 3a shows reasoning-free SFT (+22.6%/+40.4%), reasoning SFT (+6.6%/+18.1%), leaving only +15.2%/+14.0% for ADAGRPO itself, raising questions about whether extensive SFT warm-up (97.9k+23.6k steps) drives results more than algorithmic contributions
Reward model dependency: AndroidLab training uses VLM-based reward model with only 86% accuracy; best model (MobileRL-9B) avoids this by training only on AndroidWorld, limiting approach generality

Limited scope and evaluation: Only Android simulators with available verifiable rewards; no evaluation on real devices, public-use apps, or other platforms (iOS, web); limits practical generalization claims

Hyperparameter choices lack justification: Despite claiming to avoid excessive tuning, many hyperparameters (Table 4) chosen without sensitivity analysis or ablation (e.g., α=1.0, γ=1.0, κ=0.25, three-epoch cooldown)

Unfair baseline comparisons: Comparison models may not have received the same multi-stage SFT warm-up pipeline; larger models (UI-TARS-72B, UI-GENIE-72B) likely differ in training procedures, complicating fair comparison
Statistical significance incomplete: Main results (Table 1) lack confidence intervals; only three runs with uncertainty quantification shown only for training curves (Figure 11) not test performance
Reasoning SFT necessity unclear: Contributes only +1.8% on AndroidLab despite added complexity; requires off-the-shelf instruction model suggesting marginal incremental value
Computational overhead severely limits scaling: 100 training steps requires >25 hours with 4TB memory-equivalent machines and 256 concurrent rollouts; undermines practical applicability
Generalization concerns: Different training results for Qwen vs. GLM with mixed training (Table 7) suggests model-dependent approach; raises robustness questions across architectures
